Background I recently watched a video of Prof. Terry Tao’s talk at ICM 2026 that prompted me to break out of my cocoon of thoughts and pen down my own experiences with generative AI and what advancement of generative AI means for all of us.
Disclaimer Before I say any further, I would like to put up a disclosure that the content herein is an output of my mind and no help from generative AI tools was sought while writing this up. While my thoughts would and must have been influenced by a variety of factors including but not limited to generative AI, the write up itself is my own work.
My tryst with AI When I was doing my bachelors, not very long ago, RNNs and LSTMs were all the rage. AI, was still a buzzword, as much as it is now, back then. I somehow felt privileged to learn the math behind all these fancy algorithms that powered these “language models”. What was even interesting back then is the paradigm shift that the professors talked about, from symbolic AI, to frequentist models, to ML, and to more powerful general purpose language models. What my naive self could not realize back then was that the paradigm was actively shifting but in a much accelerated manner. Fast forward to my master’s (which again was not really long ago!), I came across this paper that said something about “Transformers” with a catchy title (it will be too clichéd to write the full title of the paper as you know what it is :D). This one sounded way more complicated than RNNs but thanks to the wonderful professors at the university I could comprehend a thing or two about it. In all the time that passed by, advancements in computing coupled with some really fancy systems engineering, brought AI into the market for human trials (as I see it). Like every major invention it started getting commoditized. In a matter of few months the models kept getting better at almost everything what was previously cherished and coveted as a product of human endeavor: art, prose, code, and now math (I could have categorized everything into art though). What sounded fantastical at first became the norm in no matter of time. Much to my chagrin, I find it really annoying to read messages and emails sent by “humans” that are generated by AI these days.
Destination vs journey Now that is a segway to what I really want to talk about: what does it mean to be human in the world of AI? We instinctively know whether something is written by AI. Our brains are wired and trained enough to recognize patterns that are specific to human creation. While AI does a fantastic job (kudos!) at generating fluent essays on answering a simple question such as, “How is the weather today?, it gives itself off by its sycophantic style of writing. Maybe we are wired to be willing to hear a yes or no answer sometimes while expecting to willingly hear a long rant (such as this one) when there is no absolute reason to! These imperfections and whimsical tastes of the human mind is probably what differentiates humans from AI. We are bad, no, rather horrible, at optimization. Our journey to a destination, which may be a literal destination like the sunny shores of California, or the breezy monsoons of Dharwad, or a decision in life, probably makes a profound impact on our minds more than the destination itself. The way we get to those destinations, things we see, hear, learn, and adapt along the way, is what shapes us, and our narrative. AI can at best read through millions of such documented narratives and provide a glorious account of its own journey but it for sure cannot experience one. Do note many of these journies are not perfect. Some hurt us, some make us laugh, some make us feel contended and grateful, while others leave us yearning for more. These imperfections, or perturbations from optimality, are what I consider the hallmarks of human nature, which get reflected in the works created by humans. Now clearly, enumerating all such possible perturbations or journeys and making AI read through those is an impossible task, not because AI cannot do it, but because humans cannot write everything down or coherently describe their experiences in the first place. So I theorize this is possibly why we can differentiate text generated by AI from what a human writes, as our brains are “tuned” to infer information from these imperfections and “expect” such in human generated prose.
Skills (not skills.md xp) This brings me to question: among the list of skills I have garnered and worked upon over time, what is the subset of those skills that would be “more” important than the rest, in this world flooded with news of AI? While I have deliberately tried to make this statement sound precise, in rather mathematical-sounding ’lingo’, that specific wording carries meaning. Whatever we do in life carries some meaning, whether or not explicit.
First comes critical thinking. The way we approach a problem. I always could not help but wonder, how on earth did people even think of something as …
